title: Cock-a-Leekie
subtitle: Scottish chicken and leek broth with prunes and pearl barley
excerpt: Cock-a-leekie is the national soup of Scotland: a chicken broth made with leeks and, in the traditional version, prunes. The prunes sound incongruous but they give the soup a faintly sweet, slightly tart edge that makes the broth more complex than it first appears. It is a gentle, warming soup that makes the most of a whole chicken.
sourceNotes: Cock-a-leekie is documented in Scottish recipe collections from the sixteenth century. The prunes were a standard ingredient in the earliest versions. Modern versions frequently omit them, but the soup is more interesting with them included.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the soup without the prunes. Add fresh soaked prunes when reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before. Refrigerate and skim the fat from the surface before reheating.

content.text: Cock-a-leekie builds its broth by simmering a whole chicken for 90 minutes with leeks, barley, and herbs. The chicken is lifted out, the meat shredded and returned, and the prunes added at the end to warm through. The resulting soup is clear and golden with a warmth from the leeks and a barely detectable sweetness from the prunes.

items.prepNote: washed, half sliced into 1 cm rounds, half chopped roughly for the broth

content.text: Put the whole chicken in a large pot. Add the roughly chopped half of the leeks, the bay leaves, and the thyme. Cover with about 2.5 litres of cold water. Bring to a simmer, skim the foam, and cook for 1 hour. Add the pearl barley if using and simmer for a further 30 minutes.
Lift out the chicken. Strain the broth and discard the spent leeks, bay leaves, and thyme. Return the broth to the pot. Add the sliced leeks and simmer for 15 minutes.

When the chicken is cool enough to handle, pull the meat from the bones in large pieces. Discard the skin and carcass. Return the chicken to the broth. Add the prunes and warm through for 5 minutes. Season generously with salt and pepper. Serve with chopped parsley.

items.cause: The chicken boiled too hard, or the foam was not skimmed.
items.fix: Simmer gently from the start. Skim all foam in the first 15 minutes. A clear broth should shimmer, not boil.

items.cause: The chicken was cooked too long.
items.fix: 1 hour of simmering is enough for a 1.5 kg bird. Check by pressing the leg meat , it should be very tender and pull away easily from the bone.

items.symptom: The prunes have dissolved into the soup
items.cause: They were added too early and simmered too long.
items.fix: Add the prunes in the last 5 minutes only. They should be warm and slightly soft but still intact.

items.symptom: The soup is bland after straining
items.cause: The chicken stock was weak, or the broth was not seasoned at the end.
items.fix: Season generously after straining. The barley absorbs salt as it cooks and the broth will need more than you expect.

content.text: Cock-a-leekie is mentioned in the writings of Robert Burns and is considered Scotland's national soup alongside Scotch broth. The prune addition divides opinion sharply, but the earliest documented versions all include them, and the soup is more complex and interesting for it. The sweetness is not dominant; it is a background note that makes the leek and chicken flavours more vivid.
